title: The Winter Ingvar Kamprad Went to Warsaw Looking for Chairs
dek: Shut out by Sweden's furniture trade, IKEA's founder wrote to a Polish minister and came home with a supplier and, he later said, the start of a drinking problem.

story.event: Turning to Polish factories after Swedish furniture dealers organised a supplier boycott
story.summary: Through the 1950s Sweden's furniture retailers' association pressed manufacturers not to supply IKEA, whose low prices undercut the trade, and Ingvar Kamprad was barred from trade fairs. Short of furniture, he wrote to Poland's foreign trade minister and in January 1961 visited Warsaw and a chair factory in Radomsko, placing IKEA's first Polish orders. Poland became a major, cheaper source of IKEA furniture; Kamprad later traced his long struggle with drinking to the vodka that accompanied those deals.
paragraphs: Through the 1950s, furniture makers who sold to Ingvar Kamprad risked losing their other customers. His company, IKEA, sold from a catalogue and a showroom in Älmhult, in southern Sweden, at prices rivals said were ruining the market. By IKEA's own history, the furniture retailers' association was warning suppliers as early as 1952: sell to IKEA and our members stop buying from you. Kamprad was also barred from trade fairs.

A few manufacturers kept supplying him quietly, selling discontinued models, using other names or delivering to a neutral address, and Kamprad set up a separate purchasing company. It was not enough. Danish suppliers could not fill the gap either. By the company's later account, in 1961 IKEA expected to need about 40,000 dining chairs and could source only half.

In 1960 Kamprad read that Poland's foreign trade minister was coming to Stockholm in search of Swedish business. He wrote to him and, a couple of months later, was invited. In January 1961 he travelled to Warsaw with his father, Feodor, his head of purchasing, Ragnar Sterte, and the designer Bengt Ruda. Officials at first refused them entry to any factory, until a manager, Marian Grabinski, arranged permission, and the next day they visited a chair factory in Radomsko. They ordered chairs, tables and fabrics; IKEA and Polish press accounts put the first order at 500 bentwood chairs.

Polish prices were close to half the Swedish equivalent, but quality lagged. IKEA offered long contracts, showed factories how to cut costs and brought in tools. "Slowly, and with constant setbacks, we helped to build up a modern furniture industry," Kamprad said later. Poland became one of IKEA's biggest sources of furniture, and the boycott, as the New York Times later put it, backfired.

It cost him something too. Kamprad later said his drinking problem began with the vodka that went with almost every business deal in Poland, and for decades he relied on regular spells of drying out. Of the boycott itself he said: "The boycott only made us stronger, and the crisis became a non-crisis as we were constantly coming up with new solutions."

quote.text: Plagues, troubles, fears, and cares, of various degree, All spring from many sides, and fix themselves in thee. Bear all with patience; slowly thou'lt experience gain.
quote.locator: Book I, Story V, "The Lion and the Beasts", couplets 144-145
quote.source_title: The Mesnevi, tr. Sir James W. Redhouse, Project Gutenberg eBook #61724
quote.connection: Rumi promises slow gain to those who bear their troubles patiently, and Kamprad's Polish suppliers bore that out. But Rumi also says troubles fix themselves in us. One of the troubles that came with the solution stayed with Kamprad for decades, and the gain does not cancel it.

reflection: Kamprad's answer to being shut out was to look further than anyone expected, and it worked. The story also shows that a way round an obstacle brings its own habits. The trip that solved the chair shortage came with a drinking habit that, by his own account, stayed with him for decades.

When something blocks you, you will probably find a way round it; determined people usually do. It is worth asking, while you are still choosing the route, what it will ask of your body, your evenings and the people at home, and whether you would accept that cost if you could see it plainly.
invitation: Think of one way round an obstacle that you have settled into this year, such as a late night, an extra coffee or a skipped meal. Write down what it costs you each week, then decide whether to keep paying it.

research_notes: Boycott dates differ: the IKEA Museum says the retailers' association was threatening suppliers 'as early as 1952' and elsewhere calls the boycott one 'instigated ... in the mid-1950s'; the BBC (2000) says the late 1950s; the Guardian says the 1950s and 1960s. The story says 'Through the 1950s' and dates the threats to 1952 'by IKEA's own history'. Details of the 1960 letter, the January 1961 party, the initial refusal and Marian Grabinski come from IKEA's own museum history alone and are told as such; the 1961 Radomsko order is independently confirmed by Bankier (citing IKEA, 2021), Forbes Polska and Eurobuild CEE. One Polish chamber-of-commerce page (now dead) said Radom; all other sources say Radomsko. Order size: Bankier and Forbes Polska both say 500 chairs (Forbes adds that the order later rose to 20,000; Bankier names the ÖGLA chair and 69,000 kronor); the IKEA Museum's 40,000-chair estimate is the company's own and is attributed. Price gap: the IKEA Museum says 'almost 50% lower'; the story says 'close to half'. Drinking: the BBC (2000) reports Kamprad saying his vodka habit came from the drinking that accompanied deals in Poland; the Guardian says it began there and that he dried out for three weeks once a year; the NYT says he dried out three times a year. The story says only 'regular spells of drying out'. Kamprad's past: the NYT obituary reports that he joined Per Engdahl's fascist movement in 1942, stayed close to Engdahl after 1945 and wrote in 1950 that he was proud of his involvement; Expressen revealed this in 1994 and he apologised to staff, calling it, in the NYT's translation, 'the most stupid mistake of my life'. Reuters (via Business Standard) describes the New Swedish Movement as a far-right group. As the assignment allowed, the story tells the boycott episode on its own and does not mention this, so no claim about it appears in the text. The Wprost interview in which Kamprad recalled criticism in Sweden for dealing with communist Poland, the NYT original, Reuters and The Economist were blocked to automated requests and are not cited. The Rumi couplet numbers follow the marginal numbering (every fifth couplet) in Redhouse's text.
